chunk_findings.detail: `adopt` calls `CL._claim_once(...)` and then unconditionally adds the recover-surface success keys (`found`, `_render`, `count=1`) without checking whether the claim succeeded. If `_claim_once` refuses after the earlier checks — for example, another process renews/claims the lease between the `L.scan` measurement and `_claim_once`, or the claim implementation rejects the forced takeover — the returned outcome is still a refusal, but its `data` now says `count == 1`. The comment states that the recover surface’s caps and renderer read these keys, so a failed adoption can be rendered/counted as one recovered item even though no lease was adopted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/recover_adopt.py:69-73

chunk_findings.detail: The `--adopt` branch is entered before any handling of `--plan` and calls `ddflow.api.recover_adopt.adopt` directly, without passing or checking `plan`. The declared `--plan` parameter is documented as the recovery dry run, while `--adopt` is documented to take over the lease. Thus `ddflow recover --item X --adopt --plan --reason "..."` is accepted and performs the takeover even though the user requested the dry-run/plan path; the `--plan` flag is silently ignored. A surface that exposes a dry-run flag should either reject `--adopt --plan` or propagate the dry-run request, not mutate state while pretending to plan.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/reporting.py:_recover_call

chunk_findings.detail: `adopt` returns `CL._claim_once(...)` unchanged, so a successful takeover has the claim outcome's kind, not `recover.adopt`. `render_recover` only special-cases `out.kind == "recover.adopt"` (the pre-claim `_refuse` path). Given a clean expired lease and a successful claim, the CLI falls through to `_render_recover` on claim-shaped data (and the injected `found`/`count`/`_render` keys), so the operator does not get the adoption line and can get a sweep render or a render error after the lease was already taken. A `_claim_once` refusal is likewise not `recover.adopt`, so the claim failure is not shown as an adopt refusal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/recover_adopt.py:74

chunk_findings.detail: Expiry and cleanliness are checked, then the mutation is `_claim_once(..., force=True)` with no second liveness check. `force` is what skips "held by someone else". Sequence: lease is past grace, `adopt` passes `lease.live` and the scan, the holder heartbeats and the lease is live again, then `force=True` still runs. That steals a live lease — the case the function text says it refuses — and reopens the agent force-takeover B49 closed, without `--approval`.

chunk_findings.detail: `adopt` calls `CL._claim_once(..., force=True)` after a non-atomic expired-lease check. If two agents call `recover --adopt` for the same expired lease, both can load state and pass `lease.live(...) == False`; the first claim succeeds, but the second still issues a forced claim and can overwrite the newly live lease. The module promises that a live lease is refused and nothing changes, but this interleaving changes a lease after it became live.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/recover_adopt.py:71-75

chunk_findings.detail: After calling `_claim_once`, `adopt` unconditionally sets `out.data["count"]` to `1` without checking whether the claim actually succeeded. If `_claim_once` returns a refused outcome (for example, because the worktree became dirty after `L.scan` or the claim layer rejects the takeover), the returned outcome still reports `data["count"] == 1`, so any cap/renderer that uses `count` can report one adopted item even though none was adopted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/recover_adopt.py:71-75

chunk_findings.detail: When `--adopt` is present, `_recover_call` immediately calls `ddflow.api.recover_adopt.adopt` and never honors `a.get("plan")` (or `a.get("all")`). The existing `--plan` parameter is documented as “The triage, dry run,” so a user who runs `ddflow recover --item X --adopt --plan --reason "test"` expects no state change, but this code still performs the lease takeover and records it. The dry-run flag is silently ignored; the combination should be rejected or the plan flag should be passed through to prevent mutation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/reporting.py:_recover_call

chunk_findings.detail: The seeded `task.added` event for T1 has only `parent`, `title`, and `globs`; it does not state `needs` or carry a wave tag such as `no-deps`. The recorded rule [r-task-phase-needs-wave] says every task must name its phase, state dependencies in `needs`, and carry a `wave:N` tag, with no-prerequisite tasks explicitly tagged `no-deps` so that “none” is a decision rather than an omission. This change files a task in the ddflow log without that required metadata, so the test fixture violates the project rule.

chunk_findings.detail: `adopt` returns the `_claim_once` outcome unchanged and never sets `out.kind` to `KIND` (`"recover.adopt"`). `render_recover` only prints the takeover line when `out.kind == "recover.adopt"` (`ddflow/surfaces/parsers/reporting.py:31`). After a clean expired tree is adopted, that branch is unreachable, so the surface falls through to `_render_recover` on the injected empty `found` / `_render` payload and reports a no-op sweep instead of who took the lease.

chunk_findings.detail: `growth` measures the current file with `(repo / rel).stat().st_size`, but measures the base with `git cat-file -s base:rel`; these are not the same quantity for non-regular repository entries or files affected by checkout filters. For example, if the base commit and the worktree both contain a symlink `foo.py -> bar.py`, and `bar.py` is 100,000 bytes while `limit` is 20,000, then a touched `foo.py` in `changed` gives `size == 100000`, but `_base_size` returns the blob size of the symlink (the target path length, well under the limit). `growth` then reports `foo.py` as “over the limit: split it into a package” even though the worktree file was already oversized at the base and did not grow. This violates the function’s own claim that an untouched offender passes; both sides of the comparison should be repository blob sizes, or both should be worktree sizes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/file_size.py:growth / _base_size

chunk_findings.detail: The `except OSError:  # deleted` clause treats every `stat` failure as a deletion and returns no violation. A changed `.py` path can exist but be unstatable for reasons other than deletion, e.g. a symlink loop `foo.py -> foo.py` causes `os.stat` to raise `OSError` (`ELOOP`), or a transient filesystem/permission error can raise `OSError`. In those cases `growth` silently continues and returns `[]`, i.e. it passes a check that could not run, contrary to the docstring’s “a check that could not run is never a pass.” It should catch `FileNotFoundError` (and perhaps symlink-related cases deliberately) instead of all `OSError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/file_size.py:growth

chunk_findings.detail: The “baselined” part of this test is vacuous. The baseline entry is written with the same size as the committed base file (`size = (repo / "old.py").stat().st_size` before the worktree edit), so a `growth()` implementation that never reads `FS.BASELINE` and only compares the worktree against `HEAD` still produces the expected `"grew"` message. A concrete counterexample is an implementation that ignores the baseline entirely; this test still passes, so it does not refute the claim that the ratchet uses recorded per-file sizes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_file_size_ratchet.py:test_growth_rejects_a_file_already_over_the_limit_that_grew_baselined_or_not

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that the returned message contains `"big.py"`. The stated intent requires a split-plan task per offender, but if `FS.growth()` returns only `"big.py is over the limit"` without any `"split"` instruction, this test still passes. Thus the suite does not enforce the split-plan requirement for the new-oversized-file offender.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_file_size_ratchet.py:test_growth_rejects_a_new_oversized_file

chunk_findings.detail: The “never edits ... baseline” promise is only checked when `limit` is zero, where `growth()` is supposed to return early. If a positive-limit rejection path created or updated `FS.BASELINE`, this test would not notice because it never runs the positive-limit path and then checks the baseline file. A bug where `growth(repo, ["old.py"], FIXTURE_LIMIT, "HEAD")` writes a baseline entry on rejection would pass this test suite.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_file_size_ratchet.py:test_growth_is_off_at_limit_zero_and_never_edits_a_limit_or_baseline

chunk_findings.detail: `growth` treats an unreadable path as a deleted file and returns success. `stat` OSError is swallowed, so a check that never saw the bytes still returns `[]`. Given `changed=["api/review.py"]`, base blob already over `limit` and larger than the previous blob, and a sparse checkout, bare repo, or skip-worktree where `api/review.py` is not on disk, the loop `continue`s and the merge check passes. That breaks the stated rule that a measurement that could not run is never a pass; only a missing `base` rev raises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/file_size.py:growth

chunk_findings.detail: Working-tree `stat().st_size` is compared to `git cat-file -s` blob size. Those differ under `core.autocrlf`, `text=auto`, or a clean/smudge filter. Given a grandfathered `old.py` whose blob is 25000 bytes (over a 20000 limit) and a checkout that only expands LF to CRLF so `stat` is 26000, with `changed=["old.py"]` and no content edit, `size > before` is true and the ratchet reports growth. The reverse (smudge shrinks the worktree, index blob grew) is a false pass.

chunk_findings.detail: The modified test still does not exercise the baseline in a way that distinguishes a baseline-aware ratchet from one that ignores `FS.BASELINE`. The baseline line is written with `size - 50`, i.e. below both the base blob size (`size`) and the current worktree size (`size + 1`). For example, with HEAD `old.py` at 100 bytes, worktree `old.py` at 101 bytes, and baseline `old.py | 50 | legacy`, an implementation that never reads the baseline and only compares the worktree against HEAD still returns a `"grew"` message, so all assertions pass. To catch a ratchet that ignores or mishandles the baseline, the baseline would need to be set at a value that would change the result if honored, such as at or above the current size.
